content: Lying-in is an antiquated childbirth practice where a woman remains in bed for a designated period before giving birth. While the term today is generally understood to describe the state of a woman actively in labor, historically, it referred to a mandatory period of bed rest, even in the absence of medical complications. A publication from 1932 describes the lying-in period as lasting anywhere from two weeks to two months. It also advises against getting up—that is, leaving the bed—within at least nine days postpartum, with an ideal recommendation of remaining in bed for up to 20 days. This extended period of post-birth bed rest was also referred to as lying-in. During the time when the term lying-in was more commonly used, it was often incorporated into the names of hospitals. For instance, the Royal Women’s Hospital in Australia was originally named the Melbourne Lying-In Hospital and Infirmary for Diseases of Women and Children.
